PARALLAX

Beyond the frame.

Your camera records in two dimensions. How does editing software recover the third?

Imagine adding a glowing portal to a window in a video. As the camera moves around the building, the portal needs to stay on that window, turn with the wall, and appear smaller when the camera moves farther away. After Effects’ 3D Camera Tracker helps editors do this by estimating how the camera moved and where features in the scene sit in three dimensions. PARALLAX lets you place the portal, step outside the footage, and inspect the image measurements that hold it there. Pick a scene and add an effect of your own.

FIELD NOTES

How it works

Watch the portal’s rim

Place a portal on a window corner and play the orbit. Pause when you see the wall at an angle, then switch between 2D and 3D tracking. In 2D, the rim stays round. In 3D, it looks like a narrower oval as you see it from the side.

One frame gives a direction

The software finds the window corner in a frame and records its pixel coordinates. Using those coordinates and the lens setting, it calculates a line of sight from the camera toward the corner. A corner above and to the right of the image center lies somewhere along a line pointing up and right from the camera. Its distance along that line is still unknown.

A second view reveals depth

The software finds the same corner in a frame taken from a different camera position. Now it has two lines of sight, one from each position. Once it knows or estimates how the camera moved, it calculates where those lines pass closest to each other. That gives it an estimate of the corner’s 3D position.

How 3D tracking draws the portal

When you place the portal, its center is anchored at the corner’s estimated 3D position. For each new frame, the software uses the camera’s position and viewing direction to calculate where the center and each point on the rim should appear on screen. This calculation is called projection. It’s why the center stays on the window while the rim appears narrower as the camera rounds the building.

How 2D tracking moves the portal

In 2D mode, the window corner controls where the portal’s center appears on screen. If the corner moves 8 pixels left, the center and every point on the rim move 8 pixels left together. The portal changes position while keeping its original size, shape, and orientation.

When the window goes out of view

The observatory checks visibility separately. When the building blocks the selected corner, PARALLAX stops drawing the portal. When the corner becomes visible again, the 2D portal reappears with the same shape at the corner’s new screen position.

What this experiment knows about the camera

The observatory uses a fixed lens and a programmed camera path. The tracker works from the rendered images. Uploaded clips use an assumed focal length and estimated camera motion. Their depths are relative because the pixels cannot tell us how many meters the camera traveled. Moving subjects, zoom or too few distinctive corners can spoil a solve.

After Effects provides a full camera-tracking workflow. This lab isolates the geometry behind it. Adobe’s 3D Camera Tracker guide
